title: Calling the council
hookLine: after the Buddha's passing a monk says now we can do as we like, and Kassapa calls the elders to recite the teaching together (DN 16; Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)

lines: NOW WE CAN DO AS WE LIKE.
cards: Kassapa is on the road with a large company of monks when a traveler brings the news: the teacher has died. Some monks fall to the ground weeping. Others, calmer, say that all things that come together come apart.
Then one monk, named Subhadda, says something else. Enough, friends. Don't grieve.
We're free of the great ascetic now. He was always telling us this is allowed, this isn't. From now on we can do as we like.
The long discourse on the Buddha's last days records that sentence. And Kassapa is listening.

teach.b: In the Vinaya, after the funeral, Kassapa tells the monks what Subhadda said, and proposes: let us recite the teaching and the discipline together, before what isn't the teaching starts to shine and what is starts to fade.
It's not panic; it's foresight. One careless sentence on a road showed how a teaching could bend once its teacher was gone. Second, the choosing.
The monks ask him to choose the elders, and the Vinaya numbers them at five hundred, with Ananda among them.

They agree to spend the rains in Rajagaha, and that no one else will settle there that season, so the work can go on undisturbed. Third, the work. First, the text says, they spend time repairing the dwellings.
Then they meet, and the teaching is asked for, recited and agreed, piece by piece, so it can be carried in many voices. Fourth, what kind of leadership this is.
Kassapa isn't trying to become the new Buddha; the texts don't give him that place.
He's gathering people around something bigger than any one of them.
The forest monk who wanted almost nothing for himself turned out to want one thing very much: that the teaching wouldn't be lost.

how: Theravada tradition counts the gathering at Rajagaha as the first council, and later councils, including modern ones in Myanmar, gathered monks to recite and check the texts together in the same spirit.

o: a reciting together of the teaching
a monk's vow to stay silent for life
a song sung at the Buddha's funeral

p: now we can do as we like
let us recite the teaching together
where the elders spend the rains

s: every monk wept when the news came
some wept, some were calm, and one, Subhadda, said now they could do as they liked.
Kassapa called the council to recite the teaching before it faded
he worried that what isn't the teaching would shine and what is would fade.
Kassapa made himself the new Buddha
the texts don't give him that place; he gathers the elders around the teaching.

games.q: you're Kassapa. the teacher has died, and a monk says now we can do as we like. what do you do?
o: say nothing; it's a time for grief.
gather the elders to recite the teaching together.
games.why: after the funeral he proposes reciting the teaching and discipline together, before the true teaching fades.

practice: Think of something good that could slip away if nobody tends it: a family recipe, a grandparent's stories, the way someone you lost used to do things.
Then think of two or three people who also care about it, and picture sitting down together, just once, to say it out loud and keep it. Let the idea settle, then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Sangiti. The reciting together Kassapa calls the elders to hold after the Buddha's passing, so the teaching won't fade. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali sangiti: the word for these councils, a reciting together of the teaching.

carryVoice: Your line: so it isn't lost. One careless sentence started it; a room full of voices kept the teaching. Rest well.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), the news reaching Kassapa and Subhadda's remark
